name: Kronos (CoinOpAI)

hlido_opinion.headline: A pay-per-call market-context API for agents that repeatedly refuses to be a trading signal — the disclaimers are the most credible thing on the page.
hlido_opinion.body: Kronos sells structured crypto-market context to agents over x402 on Base mainnet: a conformally-calibrated 80% price range, a risk/cooldown state, a decision journal that returns a decision_id, and an audit endpoint that later checks the outcome against real prices. The product's own framing does the heavy lifting on credibility. It says outright that Kronos is not a buy/sell oracle, repeats twice that directional values are supporting context rather than trade instructions, and organises the whole loop around verification — preflight, decision, audit — under the line "trust the process less, verify the record more". In a category built on implied certainty, an API whose central feature is a calibrated interval and an auditable record is a meaningfully better design. The agent-readiness is also concrete: per-endpoint pricing down to half a cent, a published OpenAPI document, and an llms.txt. The reservations are real. Calibration is asserted ("~0.80 empirical coverage") with no published backtest, sample size, or period; there is no named team, track record, or third-party validation; the operator bundles an unrelated image-generation endpoint and 819 automation prompts, which muddies the focus; and the underlying domain is one where confident-sounding numbers cause real financial loss even when hedged well. Reviewed from the public surface only — we did not pay for a call.

tier_rationale: STEADY (71) for disciplined scoping and genuine agent-readiness: a calibrated range rather than a direction call, an explicit non-oracle disclaimer repeated where it matters, a verifiable preflight→decision→audit loop, per-endpoint pricing to the half-cent, plus OpenAPI and llms.txt. Held below VITAL because the calibration claim is published without any backtest, sample size or period, there is no named team or track record, and the surface mixes in unrelated image-generation and prompt-catalogue endpoints.
what_it_does_well: Leads with a calibrated 80% interval and risk state rather than a directional buy/sell call
States plainly that it is not a buy/sell oracle, and repeats that directional values are not trade instructions
Auditable loop by design — preflight, decision journal with a decision_id, then outcome verification against later prices
Per-endpoint pricing published to the half-cent, so an agent can budget before calling
Machine-readable surface: OpenAPI document and llms.txt both published and linked
x402 pay-per-call on Base mainnet — no account, no subscription, agent-native payment
what_it_fails_at: The ~0.80 empirical coverage claim is published with no backtest, sample size, time period, or methodology
No named team, operating history, or third-party validation anywhere on the surface
Focus is diluted by unrelated bundled endpoints (AI image generation, 819 automation prompts, 115 platforms)
Crypto market forecasting is a domain where even well-hedged outputs can drive real financial loss
Data freshness is surfaced as a field but no uptime, latency or availability record is published
Not tested — we did not purchase a call, so the response quality behind the pricing table is unverified
best_for: Agent developers who want structured, auditable market context rather than a signal to act on
Systems that need a decision journal and later outcome verification for compliance or post-mortem
x402-native agents that must pay per call without an account relationship
not_recommended_for: Anyone seeking trading signals or investment advice — the vendor says this is not that, and neither do we
Buyers who need published calibration evidence before relying on an interval
Use cases requiring an availability guarantee or an identifiable, accountable operator

red_flags.note: The calibration figure (~0.80 empirical coverage) is the product's central claim and is published with no supporting backtest, sample size or period. It is presented honestly as an empirical property rather than a guarantee, but a buyer cannot check it.

~0.80 empirical coverage of the calibrated range
